application.cover_letter_markdown:
Dear Hiring Team at Kaikuvaara,

I saw your advertisement for a Senior Signal Processing Engineer on the national jobs portal. My background is in secondary education rather than engineering, but I wanted to put myself forward because I have been thinking about a career change for some time and the listing caught my attention.

For the last fourteen years I have taught mathematics at Bukchon Academy in Seoul. The core of my work is straightforward classroom teaching, but the parts of the job I have found most rewarding are the ones where I have had to design something from scratch and then measure whether it actually worked.

The best example is the grade 10 problem-solving module I rewrote in 2018. The previous version had been in place for several years and was not producing the results we wanted. I spent most of a semester identifying where students were getting stuck, rewrote the materials with a much stronger emphasis on structured problem decomposition, and piloted the new version with one class before rolling it out to the full year group. Assessment scores went up by about 15 percent and the improvement held across subsequent cohorts. The revised module is still in use today, which I think is the most reliable indicator that it was genuinely an improvement rather than a one-off blip.

I have also run the school’s annual mathematics competition since 2016, which involves writing the question papers, organising the logistics for roughly 300 students, and managing all the marking and results. It is a recurring operational task and I have kept it running smoothly for eight consecutive years without significant problems. On the mentoring side, I have supervised eight student research projects for an external mathematics fair, with two of them finishing in the top ten. Those projects required working with students on unfamiliar problems under genuine time pressure, which is a very different sort of challenge from regular classroom work.

I am realistic about the gap between what I have done and what this role requires. I have no engineering background and would need substantial retraining to be useful. But I have spent fourteen years working in an environment that demands careful analytical thinking and the ability to explain complex ideas clearly, and I would like to find out whether those habits can transfer to a technical setting. If you are open to considering a non-traditional applicant, I would be grateful for the chance to discuss it further.

Pierre Berg

application.cover_letter_markdown:
To the hiring team at Kaikuvaara Oy,

After graduating from CRIT in 2024 and then spending several months recovering from a serious illness, I joined Boreal Photonics in Espoo at the start of 2025 as a signal processing engineer. I had to take further medical leave later that year and only returned to full-time work in the spring of 2026, so I am still relatively early in my time at Boreal. But the work has confirmed that signal processing is the direction I want to take, and I am now looking at what comes next.

The reason I am writing to Kaikuvaara is partly about the work and partly about where I want my career to go. Boreal has been a solid first employer, but the scope of what I do here is fairly narrow. I spend most of my time characterising optical sensors and running drift studies, which is useful and I am learning from it, but I want to work on problems that stretch me further. Kaikuvaara’s sensing instrumentation work looks like it operates at a different scale and level of complexity.

I should be direct about my limitations. I graduated less than two years ago, my degree is in biological engineering rather than electrical engineering or physics, and I have one employer on my CV. These are real gaps. What I can say is that the analytical foundations from my CRIT training have transferred to signal processing work better than I expected, and I have been learning the domain-specific material quickly at Boreal.

One practical point: Boreal’s entire technical team works in English. All my internal reports, test protocols, calibration documentation and project summaries are written in English. I have also presented interim results to the wider engineering group on two occasions, both in English. Since my degree was conducted entirely in English, none of this has been a stretch.

I relocated from the US to Finland last year, so moving within the country would be straightforward by comparison. Oulu is somewhere I would genuinely consider. Having already made one international move, the idea of settling elsewhere in Finland does not feel daunting.

I realise this application is a long shot given the seniority you are looking for, but if there is room for a conversation I would appreciate the chance.

Kristina Kowalski

- Developed the pre-processing chain for microwave sounder data from the ICEMONT-2 satellite, handling raw telemetry through to calibrated brightness temperature products
- Applied signal processing and statistical methods from my physics training to design and validate an atmospheric correction module for high-latitude data sets
- Delivered as part of a Kestrel Europe-funded consortium; worked throughout as a Finnish citizen under standard EU arrangements

application.cover_letter_markdown:
Remote sensing instrument work is what has kept me at Aurinko Avionics for seven years, and the prospect of doing more of it at Kaikuvaara is what made me write this letter. Building sensing payloads where failure is not really an option because the hardware is in orbit or flying a survey line over the Arctic – that is the kind of engineering environment I want to be in for the next stage of my career, and from what I know of Kaikuvaara’s work, it is exactly what you do.

My most technically demanding piece of beamforming work at Aurinko was on the SAFIRE-2 programme. I implemented a digital beamformer for a 16-element receive array used in an airborne ice-thickness sounder. The instrument needed to suppress strong surface returns while preserving weak basal echoes, and I wrote the beam-steering and null-placement algorithms from scratch. Getting the sidelobe levels down to the specification took several iterations of the weight computation, and the final version of the processing ran in real time during flight campaigns starting in 2021. That project taught me more about phased-array signal processing in practice than anything I had done before or since.

SAFIRE-2 also had a significant real-time processing component running on a TMS320C6748 DSP. I wrote the core decimation, filtering and detection stages in C, working within fixed-point arithmetic and a memory budget that left very little margin. Most of my embedded work at Aurinko follows a similar pattern: the processing has to keep up with the sensor data rate on hardware selected for power and thermal behaviour rather than computational headroom. It is painstaking, not glamorous, but it is the part where most of the practical problems live and I keep coming back to it.

On the tooling side, I maintain Aurinko’s Python-based ground-segment processing chain for post-flight data reduction. I inherited it as a set of ad-hoc scripts and rewrote it in 2022 as a properly structured package with unit tests, continuous integration and versioned releases. It handles the full pipeline from raw binary ingest through to calibrated geophysical products, and several other engineers at Aurinko use it routinely. I would not call myself a software developer first, but I can write production-quality Python when the work calls for it.

What draws me to Kaikuvaara specifically is the chance to work on instruments that actually go to space or fly survey missions over terrain that matters. I find this kind of work genuinely satisfying in a way I did not fully anticipate when I started in the field, and doing it from Oulu, closer to the Arctic environments these instruments are built to observe, would be a good fit.

I would be happy to discuss any of this in more detail.

Esa Jarvinen

application.cover_letter_markdown:
With over twenty-five years in signal processing and sensor systems, I bring exactly the depth and breadth that Kaikuvaara Oy needs for the Senior Signal Processing Engineer role in Oulu.

Oulu has been at the top of my list for some time now. The concentration of RF and photonics engineering talent in the region is frankly unmatched anywhere else in the Nordics, and having already spent six months on a client secondment in Tampere in 2018, I know first-hand that the Finnish engineering ecosystem is where I want to be. The Oulu cluster in particular, with its combination of established sensor companies, strong university research groups and a growing startup scene, is the kind of environment where someone with my level of experience can make the biggest impact.

My skillset covers the full spectrum of what a signal processing role demands. I bring deep expertise in embedded DSP development in C/C++, extensive RF measurement and characterisation experience, strong command of Kalman filtering and estimation theory, and significant hands-on work with satellite and airborne platform systems. Over my career I have operated across every layer of the signal chain, and I offer a unique combination of theoretical depth and practical delivery capability that is very hard to find in one engineer. My educational background gives me the foundations to tackle any signal processing challenge that comes my way, and twenty-five years of uninterrupted professional practice have turned that foundation into consistently reliable delivery.

I have also maintained an active publication record and contributed to open-source signal processing tooling throughout my career. I believe in advancing the state of the art for the benefit of the broader community, and sharing knowledge is simply part of how I work.

What really sets me apart is versatility. Most engineers at this level have specialised heavily in one area. I have not. Whether it is designing Kalman filters for a target-tracking application, specifying RF measurement protocols for a new front-end, writing firmware for resource-constrained DSP hardware, or developing processing algorithms for airborne sensor platforms, I deliver. That breadth combined with over two and a half decades of proven, continuous delivery means I can contribute meaningfully from day one, regardless of which programme area Kaikuvaara assigns me to.

I am genuinely motivated by the prospect of joining Oulu's RF and photonics community and am ready to relocate immediately. I would welcome the opportunity to discuss how my extensive signal processing background can support Kaikuvaara's mission.

Best regards,
Anneke Jensen

The concentration of sensing and photonics companies around Oulu has been on my radar for a couple of years now. When the Senior Signal Processing Engineer listing at Kaikuvaara appeared, it seemed like a good moment to make a move.

I have been at Boreal Photonics in Espoo since 2016, working on signal processing for their optical and acoustic sensor product lines. application.cover_letter_markdown:
Sumuvire Wireless has been my only employer since I came back to Finland from Seoul in 2007. Nearly twenty years in one company, all of it in Oulu, all of it signal processing for wireless sensor systems. Kaikuvaara's listing reached me through a colleague, and it sounded like exactly the kind of move I have been wanting to make: same city, same general discipline, but a different kind of problem.

The work I have done at Sumuvire is centred on one thing: getting clean, usable data out of wireless sensor channels where the conditions are working against you. Noisy environments, constrained power budgets, interference between densely packed nodes. The project I would point to first is a multi-year effort to improve the signal processing chain for Sumuvire's environmental monitoring sensors, which are deployed across forested and sub-Arctic terrain in northern Finland and Sweden. When I inherited the processing pipeline in 2014, the system was losing roughly 8 percent of transmitted readings to noise-related data corruption. I redesigned the filtering and detection stages, tested alternatives extensively in simulation, and deployed the updated algorithms in 2016. Packet loss dropped below 2 percent and has stayed there across subsequent hardware revisions and new deployment sites. That processing is still running in production today, which I think says more about it than any single number.

More recently I worked on a cross-border sensor network deployment spanning Finland, Sweden and Estonia. My contribution was the signal conditioning and interference rejection algorithms for a new generation of sensor node, plus the MATLAB-based acceptance testing tools we used before each site rollout. The project ran from 2018 to 2020 and the network has been in continuous operation since.

These are not headline results. Nobody is going to write a press release about cutting packet loss from 8 to 2 percent. But they represent the kind of steady, measurable improvement that keeps production sensing systems running, and that is what I think matters most in this line of work. I am good at finding the parts of a signal chain that should work better and then making them work better. Nineteen years of doing this helps.

What attracts me to Kaikuvaara is the shift from communication infrastructure to sensing instruments. At Sumuvire, signal processing has always been a supporting function inside a wireless product. Moving to a company where the signal processing is closer to the core of what the product does and how well it performs would be a welcome change.

I am available for an interview whenever suits and happy to provide references from Sumuvire.

Matti Kinnunen

Amir Tanaka
Tallinn, Estonia

EDUCATION

Charles River Institute of Technology (CRIT)
SB Electrical Engineering (2007)

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

Signal Processing Engineer
Baltic Sensor Networks, Tallinn, Estonia
2008 – present (career break 2010–2011 for further study)

- Embedded DSP development in C for radar receiver modules; wrote the matched filter and pulse compression processing stages for a TI C6678 multi-core DSP, meeting real-time throughput requirements at pulse repetition frequencies up to 10 kHz
- Conducted RF path characterisation for new receiver front-ends using calibrated spectrum analysers and signal generators, verifying gain flatness, phase linearity and image rejection across the 1–4 GHz operating band
- Based in Tallinn; spent three months on secondment to a client site in Oulu in 2019 for radar system integration; prepared to relocate to Oulu permanently

PROJECTS

SENSORIA Ground Weather Radar (Baltic Sensor Networks, 2017–2020)
- Led a team of four signal processing engineers in designing and delivering the receive processing chain for ground-based weather radars deployed at three Baltic sites under Kestrel 2020 funding
- Applied optimal signal detection methods developed during undergraduate research at CRIT to redesign the clutter rejection algorithm, achieving approximately 40% false alarm rate reduction in coastal environments without degrading detection probability
- Estonian long-term resident with full EU work authorisation; served as Baltic's lead technical contributor to this four-country consortium

Maritime Surveillance Radar – CFAR Upgrade (2013–2015)
- Redesigned the constant false-alarm-rate detector for Baltic's maritime surveillance radar to handle cluttered near-shore environments
- Updated detector has been in continuous production use since 2015

SKILLS

- Phased-array beamforming (developed adaptive null-steering algorithms for Baltic's 32-element L-band receive array, operational since 2016)
- Radar signal processing (detection, waveform design, clutter mitigation)
- Embedded real-time signal processing (TI C6000 family)
- MATLAB, Simulink
- Statistical signal detection
- Open-source contributions and publications
application.cover_letter_markdown:
I have been at Baltic Sensor Networks in Tallinn since 2008, working on ground-based radar systems. The signal processing experience I have built here, from algorithm development through embedded implementation to field deployment, translates directly to what I understand Kaikuvaara's work to involve.

The largest project I have delivered was SENSORIA, a Kestrel 2020 programme building ground-based weather radars across the Baltic region. I led the signal processing team for Baltic's contribution: four engineers, a two-year schedule, three operational sites to deliver. We finished on time and the systems have been running since 2020 with minimal maintenance intervention. That project is probably the clearest evidence I can offer that I can carry a radar signal processing problem from requirements through to deployed, working hardware and keep it running afterwards.

Before SENSORIA, most of my time went into Baltic's maritime surveillance radar. The problem I spent the longest on was false alarm performance in cluttered coastal environments. The original CFAR detector was adequate in open water but generated far too many false targets near shorelines and harbour structures. I reworked the clutter map and threshold adaptation, drawing on detection theory I had studied at CRIT, and brought the false alarm rate down by roughly 40 percent without meaningful loss in detection probability. It took close to a year of iteration and two firmware revision cycles, but the updated processing shipped in 2015 and is still in production.

On the practical side, most of my daily work is on the receive chain. I wrote the matched filtering and pulse compression stages running on our TI C6678 DSP boards, and I handle the RF characterisation each time a new front-end design arrives from the hardware group. These tasks are where most of the real engineering problems show up. Not glamorous, but that is where I have become most useful.

I took a career break in 2010–2011 to pursue further study. The gap is there in my timeline and I am not going to explain it away. I came back to Baltic and have been here without interruption since.

Regarding logistics: I hold an Estonian long-term residence permit and have full right to work anywhere in the EU. I have been in Tallinn for almost eighteen years but am ready to relocate. I spent three months in Oulu on a client secondment in 2019 and liked the city. The concentration of sensing and RF companies there is a genuine draw, and I want the signal processing to be the critical path in what I work on, not a supporting subsystem inside a larger platform.

I can make myself available at short notice for an interview.

Amir Tanaka

Aleksandra Dubois
Tampere, Finland
aleksandra.dubois@mail.example

EDUCATION

Rheinmark Technical University Aachen, Germany
MSc Electrical Engineering (2014)

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

Signal Processing Engineer
Tuulikallio Embedded Systems, Tampere
June 2015 – present

- Developed and maintained production Python pipelines for satellite payload telemetry reduction and automated signal processing, supporting two EORA-contracted instrument programmes (2019–present)
- RF measurement and characterisation of receiver front-end modules using vector network analysers and spectrum analysers; responsible for verifying gain, noise figure, phase linearity and spurious-free dynamic range prior to payload integration
- Signal processing algorithm development for spaceborne and airborne remote sensing instruments, including contributed processing for the VIIMA-2 hyperspectral imaging payload (Finnish Orbital Programme Office, 2020–2023) and an airborne ice-sounding radar funded through Kestrel Europe
- Co-authored three peer-reviewed papers at SESE IGRSS (2021, 2022, 2024); maintain an open-source spectral calibration toolkit on GitHub (~120 stars)
- French national, EU citizen; employed continuously in Finland since 2015
- All technical deliverables, consortium reports and client documentation written in English; presented results at IGRSS and at internal programme reviews in English

SKILLS

- Signal processing and spectral analysis
- Production Python (NumPy, SciPy, pytest, CI/CD)
- MATLAB, Simulink
- RF test and measurement instrumentation
- Remote sensing data processing
- Location: Tampere. Available to relocate to Oulu; have attended industry events there regularly and am familiar with the city.
application.cover_letter_markdown:
Kaikuvaara came up in conversation at the Oulu Sensing and Space Forum last November, and I have been watching your openings since. The RF and photonics engineering community in Oulu is compact enough that people genuinely know each other's work, which is not something I can say about Tampere. When the Senior Signal Processing Engineer listing appeared, applying was straightforward.

My most directly relevant recent work at Tuulikallio has been on phased-array receive processing for ground-based weather radars. I designed the digital beamforming pipeline for a 24-element receive array, taking raw ADC output through to formed beams with adaptive sidelobe control. The key difficulty was keeping processing latency within budget for real-time volume scanning during convective weather, and the solution involved overlapping the spatial FFT with the data acquisition cycle. That system has been running at two Finnish Atmosphere Survey Institute sites since 2023.

A separate project that stretched me in a different direction was about eighteen months of work on sensor-fusion firmware for drone flight controllers, under a Tuulikallio subcontract with a Finnish UAV manufacturer. The task was combining IMU, barometric and magnetometer inputs into stable navigation outputs on an STM32 microcontroller, working within hard real-time timing constraints and very limited memory. We certified the output against the manufacturer's flight-safety requirements, which meant extensive testing under simulated fault conditions. That project taught me the most about working within tight resource budgets on constrained hardware.

My MSc at Rheinmark TU Aachen was in electrical engineering with a specialisation in communications and signal processing. My thesis dealt with wideband direction-of-arrival estimation for sensor arrays, which turned out to be the theoretical foundation for nearly all the array processing work I have done professionally. The connection between that academic grounding and what I do in practice has been unusually direct.

Oulu is where I want to be next. The combination of Kaikuvaara's instrument work, the local research groups and the broader sensing industry makes it more appealing than Tampere for the next stage of my career. I hold EU citizenship and relocating would be straightforward. I would welcome the chance to visit and discuss the position.

Aleksandra Dubois
